notes.title: Sets and the inclusion–exclusion principle
notes.body: For finite sets, |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|: adding both counts double-counts the overlap. Worked example: A=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5], B=[4, 5, 6, 7]. |A|=5, |B|=4, A∩B=[4, 5] so |A∩B|=2. Then |A∪B| = 5+4−2 = **7**, and indeed A∪B=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] has **7** elements. The formula and the enumeration agree. Use it whenever two counted groups overlap — double-counting is the classic off-by-error in combinatorics.

notes.title: Counting: product and sum rules
notes.body: Product rule: if a task has a choices for step 1 and b for step 2, there are a×b combined outcomes. Sum rule: for disjoint alternatives, add. Worked example: a password of 2 letters then 3 digits. Letters: 26^2 = 676; digits: 10^3 = 1000; total = 676,000 by the product rule. Worked example 2: an identifier is either a 3-letter code or a 4-digit code: 26^3 + 10^4 = 27,576 by the sum rule (disjoint cases). Name the rule before computing — most counting errors are rule-selection errors, not arithmetic.

notes.title: Permutations and combinations, computed
notes.body: Ordered selections: P(n,k) = n!/(n−k)!. Unordered: C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n−k)!). Worked example: choose a 3-person committee from 10 people. C(10,3) = 10!/(3!·7!) = **120**. If the 3 roles are distinct (ordered), P(10,3) = **720**. Sanity check: C(n,k) = C(n,n−k); here C(10,3) = C(10,7) = 120 — both computed, both equal. Ask 'does order matter?' first: committees no, passwords yes. This module is the toolkit for the entire course: proofs, counting, recurrences.

notes.title: The pigeonhole principle
notes.body: If 13 items go into 12 boxes, some box holds at least ⌈13/12⌉ = **2** items. Worked example: among 13 people, at least two share a birth month (12 months). Proof by contradiction: if every month had at most one, there would be at most 12 people — contradiction. This 'obvious' principle proves real things: hash collisions are unavoidable when items exceed slots, and any lossless compression scheme fails on some input. Existence proofs without construction are a core discrete-math move.

notes.title: Induction, with a verified example
notes.body: To prove P(n) for all n ≥ 1: prove P(1) (base), then prove P(k) → P(k+1) (step). Worked example: S(n) = 1+2+…+n = n(n+1)/2. Base: S(1) = 1 = 1·2/2 ✓. Step: assume S(k)=k(k+1)/2; then S(k+1) = k(k+1)/2 + (k+1) = (k+1)(k+2)/2 ✓. Numerical verification: for n=100, formula gives 100·101/2 = **5050**, and direct summation gives **5050** — equal. Induction is how you prove loop correctness and closed forms: state the invariant, base, and step explicitly.

notes.title: Recurrences and divide-and-conquer cost
notes.body: Worked example: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n with T(1) = 1 (the mergesort shape). Unfold: each level does n work across twice as many subproblems; there are log2(n) levels. Closed form: T(n) = n·log2(n) + n. Verification at n=1024: recursion computes **11264**, closed form gives 1024·10+1024 = **11264** — exact match. This is where n log n comes from, not from memorization: count the levels, multiply by work per level. Every divide-and-conquer analysis in this course follows this template.

notes.title: Propositions and truth values
notes.body: A proposition is a statement that is either true or false, never both. `p AND q` is true only when both are true; `p OR q` is true when at least one is true; `NOT p` flips the value. Worked example: evaluate `(p AND q) OR (NOT r)` at p=T, q=F, r=T. First `p AND q` = T AND F = F. Then `NOT r` = NOT T = F. Finally `F OR F` = **F**. So the whole expression is **F**. Work inside-out: parentheses first, then NOT, then AND, then OR — the same precedence habit that prevents bugs in code conditions.

notes.title: Truth tables, computed by enumeration
notes.body: A truth table lists every assignment of the variables. With n variables there are 2^n rows — for n=3 that is **8** rows, computed as 2^3. Worked example: the implication `p -> q`, defined as `(NOT p) OR q`. Its table: p=T,q=T -> T; p=T,q=F -> F; p=F,q=T -> T; p=F,q=F -> T. The only false row is true-premise/false-conclusion. Enumerating all rows mechanically (as the lab does in Python) removes all doubt: no case is forgotten, because the count 2^n proves the table is complete.

notes.title: De Morgan's laws, verified by brute force
notes.body: De Morgan's laws: `NOT (p AND q)` equals `(NOT p) OR (NOT q)`, and `NOT (p OR q)` equals `(NOT p) AND (NOT q)`. Worked verification: checking all 4 assignments of (p,q) in Python, every row agrees — **True**. This is the law behind simplifying negated conditions: `NOT (admin AND active)` becomes `NOT admin OR NOT active`. In code and in firewall/policy rules, pushing NOT inward with De Morgan turns an unreadable negated conjunction into a plain disjunction.

notes.title: Implication and the contrapositive
notes.body: `p -> q` (if p then q) is logically equivalent to its contrapositive `(NOT q) -> (NOT p)`. Worked verification: all 4 assignments agree — **True**. The converse `q -> p` is NOT equivalent (check p=T,q=F: implication false, converse true). Practical use: to prove 'if the build passes then tests ran', prove the contrapositive 'if tests did not run then the build fails' — often the easier direction. Confusing implication with converse is one of the most common logic errors in specifications.

notes.title: Predicate logic over finite domains
notes.body: Predicates add quantifiers: `FORALL x, P(x)` and `EXISTS x, P(x)`. Over a finite domain you can evaluate them by enumeration. Worked example: domain = {2, 3, 4}, statement `EXISTS x, x is prime AND x > 3`. Check: x=2 (prime, not >3, fails), x=3 (prime, not >3, fails), x=4 (not prime, fails). No witness exists, so the statement is **false**. Change `>3` to `>=3`: x=3 is prime and >= 3, so the statement becomes **true**. Existence claims need exactly one witness; universal claims need every case. This discipline maps directly onto testing: 'there exists an input that crashes' vs 'for all inputs it terminates'.

notes.title: Boolean algebra for systems work
notes.body: Boolean algebra gives simplification laws: absorption `p OR (p AND q) = p`, distribution, idempotence `p AND p = p`. Worked example: simplify `(admin AND active) OR (admin AND NOT active)`. Factor admin: `admin AND (active OR NOT active)` = `admin AND T` = **admin**. Verified by enumerating all 4 assignments of (admin, active): both sides agree on every row. Why it matters: access-policy engines evaluate exactly these expressions. Simplifying before deploying means fewer rules, faster evaluation, and policies a human can audit. Formal systems start here: propositions, quantifiers, and what 'proof' means.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **induction** — proof by base case, inductive hypothesis, and inductive step; every recursive algorithm's correctness proof uses it — the template until it's reflex
- **loop invariant** — a property true before and after each iteration; the loop invariant proves the loop — state it before writing the loop
- **contradiction** — assume the negation of the claim, derive an absurdity; the halting proof's weapon
- **number theory** — divisibility, modular arithmetic, gcd; Fermat's little theorem and Euler's theorem — RSA's prerequisites, straight from 6.1200
- **graph theory** — the universal modeling language: vertices, edges, BFS/DFS, Dijkstra, MST
- **divide-and-conquer** — split, solve recursively, combine; analyzed via recurrences like T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)
- **master theorem** — closed form for T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n): compare f(n) against n^(log_b a) — smaller gives case 1, equal gives case 2 (times log n), larger (regularity) gives case 3; memorize the three cases, derive when unsure
- **amortized analysis** — cost averaged over a sequence of operations; three methods: aggregate, accounting, potential — dynamic-array append is O(1) amortized via doubling
- **exchange argument** — the proof pattern for greedy correctness: show an optimal solution can be transformed to include the greedy choice — greedy stays ahead (MST, scheduling)
- **lower bound** — a proof that no algorithm in a model can do better; comparison sorting is Ω(n log n) by the decision-tree argument: n! leaves need log(n!) depth
- **reduction** — to prove X hard, reduce a known-hard problem TO X in polynomial time; reduction direction matters (3-SAT ≤p X proves X hard)
- **NP-completeness** — the hardest problems in NP; 3-SAT is the canonical one — reductions start here
- **FSM** — finite-state machine: combinational logic plus state; the building block of the FSM-to-processor climb — every level is the previous level's abstraction, no magic
- **hardware/software contract** — the ISA, assembly, and calling conventions: the exact boundary the hardware promises the software
- **end-to-end argument** — implement correctness-critical functions at the endpoints, not in the network; the network can't guarantee what endpoints need
- **xv6** — MIT's teaching Unix-like kernel in ~10k lines; reading a real kernel demystifies scheduling, virtual memory, and filesystems
- **diagonalization** — self-referential construction used to prove the halting problem undecidable; the most beautiful proof in CS — learn it cold
- **P vs NP** — P: solvable in polynomial time; NP: verifiable in polynomial time; NP-complete problems are the hardest in NP; PSPACE sits beyond

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Prove and analyze an algorithm, end to end — the procedure behind the Induction Proof Workshop and the recurrence drills:
1. **State the claim precisely** — the specification: what must hold, for which inputs (e.g., sum_{i=1..n}(2i-1) = n^2).
2. **Write the loop invariant before the loop** — a property true before and after each iteration (binary search: the key, if present, lies in a[lo..hi)).
3. **Induction skeleton: BASE → HYPOTHESIS → STEP** — prove the base case, assume the hypothesis for k, derive k+1 (Bernoulli step: (1+x)^(k+1) = (1+x)^k(1+x) ≥ (1+kx)(1+x) = 1+(k+1)x+kx² ≥ 1+(k+1)x).
4. **Preserve the invariant each iteration** — binary search halves [lo,hi): if key < a[mid] set hi=mid, else lo=mid+1; the key stays inside; hi−lo shrinks, so the loop terminates.
5. **Write the recurrence** — count the work per level (mergesort: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n).
6. **Apply the master theorem** — T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n is case 2: f(n) = n = n^(log_2 2), so Θ(n log n).
7. **Check amortized cost where operations repeat** — dynamic-array append with doubling: n appends cost O(n) total, O(1) amortized each.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Formal material demands rigor. These habits corrupt understanding of Stanford: The Core Cross-Walk:
- **Hand-waving proofs.** 'Clearly' and 'obviously' are where the bugs hide. Write the invariant, the base case, and the step — fully, every time.
- **Ignoring edge cases in analysis.** Empty input, single element, duplicates, maximum size. The analysis isn't done until the edges are accounted for.
- **Confusing average with worst case.** Know which one your bound describes and which one your adversary gets to choose.
- **Notation sloppiness.** O, Theta, Omega mean different things; using them interchangeably trains fuzzy thinking. Say exactly which bound you proved.
- **Skipping the reduction.** Every new problem in Stanford: The Core Cross-Walk should be connected to something known: 'this is just X in disguise.' Reductions are how the field thinks.
- **Code without the argument.** An implementation with no written correctness or complexity argument is half a solution. The argument is the deliverable; code is the exhibit.

scriptLabs.title: Induction Proof Workshop
scriptLabs.brief: Write complete induction proofs for three claims: sum of odds, Bernoulli's inequality, and the loop invariant of binary search. The required fragments force the proof skeleton.
scriptLabs.starter:
# For each claim, write: BASE, HYPOTHESIS, STEP.
# 1. sum_{i=1..n} (2i-1) = n^2
# 2. (1+x)^n >= 1+nx for x > -1 (Bernoulli)
# 3. Binary search loop invariant: if key in a[0..n), key in a[lo..hi)
scriptLabs.hint: Bernoulli step: (1+x)^(k+1) = (1+x)^k(1+x) >= (1+kx)(1+x) = 1+(k+1)x+kx² >= 1+(k+1)x. Binary search: invariant preserved by halving.
scriptLabs.solution:
# 1. Sum of odds
# BASE: n=1: 1 = 1^2. HYPOTHESIS: sum to k = k^2.
# STEP: sum to k+1 = k^2 + (2(k+1)-1) = k^2+2k+1 = (k+1)^2. QED.
# 2. Bernoulli: BASE n=0: 1>=1. HYPOTHESIS: (1+x)^k >= 1+kx.
# STEP: (1+x)^(k+1)=(1+x)^k(1+x) >= (1+kx)(1+x) = 1+(k+1)x+kx^2 >= 1+(k+1)x. QED.
# 3. Binary search invariant: key in a[lo..hi) initially (lo=0,hi=n).
# STEP: mid=(lo+hi)//2; if a[mid]==key done; if key<a[mid] hi=mid else lo=mid+1.
# Invariant preserved: key (if present) stays in [lo,hi). Termination: hi-lo shrinks.
# QED: loop exits with key found or lo==hi (absent).

scriptLabs.title: A Tiny Allocator (15-213 Spirit)
scriptLabs.brief: Implement a bump allocator with free-list reuse in Python (simulating the malloc lab): malloc(size), free(ptr), with first-fit search and coalescing. The 15-213 lesson in miniature.
scriptLabs.hint: malloc: scan free_list for length>=n; split remainder back. free: insert sorted, merge with adjacent (coalesce). Track allocations in a dict for the demo.
scriptLabs.solution:
class MiniHeap:
    def __init__(self, size=1024):
        self.mem = bytearray(size)
        self.free_list = [(0, size)]
        self.allocd = {}
    def malloc(self, n):
        for i, (off, ln) in enumerate(self.free_list):
            if ln >= n:  # first-fit
                self.allocd[off] = n
                if ln == n:
                    self.free_list.pop(i)
                else:  # split: carve n, leave remainder
                    self.free_list[i] = (off+n, ln-n)
                return off
        return None
    def free(self, off):
        n = self.allocd.pop(off)
        self.free_list.append((off, n))
        self.free_list.sort()
        # coalesce adjacent
        merged = [self.free_list[0]]
        for o, l in self.free_list[1:]:
            po, pl = merged[-1]
            if po+pl == o:
                merged[-1] = (po, pl+l)
            else:
                merged.append((o, l))
        self.free_list = merged

h = MiniHeap(64)
a, b, c = h.malloc(16), h.malloc(16), h.malloc(16)
h.free(b)          # hole in the middle
d = h.malloc(8)    # first-fit reuses the hole, splits remainder
print('free_list:', h.free_list)  # coalescing visible
# Lesson: fragmentation is the enemy; coalescing is the defense.

answerBank.q: Which school's version should I follow?
answerBank.a: All three where they overlap — that's the point of the cross-walk. Start with MIT's order (prerequisite-clean), use CMU for systems depth (15-213/410), Stanford for the AI branches. The module sequences them.

answerBank.q: Do I really need theory for a dev job?
answerBank.a: For most CRUD work, no. For interviews at selective companies, distributed systems, databases, and performance work — yes, constantly. Theory is the highest-leverage knowledge: it doesn't expire.

answerBank.q: How do I learn proofs as a programmer?
answerBank.a: Write them like code: state the claim (spec), then the proof (implementation). Do every exercise in 6.1200/CS103 — proofs are a writing skill, and writing is learned by writing.

answerBank.q: xv6 vs Linux for learning OS?
answerBank.a: xv6 first (10k lines, every concept visible), then Linux source for the specific subsystem you need. The module uses xv6 as the reference implementation.

answerBank.q: P vs NP — should I care?
answerBank.a: As a practitioner: NP-completeness tells you when to stop searching for the perfect algorithm and start approximating. That's a career's worth of saved time in one concept.

faq.q: Do working engineers really use proofs?
faq.a: The *techniques*, constantly: invariants for tricky loops, induction for recursive code, reduction thinking for 'is this problem hard?' Full formal proofs are rarer — but the reasoning transfers everywhere.

faq.q: Why study compilers if I never write one?
faq.a: Because you debug their output daily: optimization surprises, undefined behavior, link errors, and performance cliffs all become legible once you know the phases.

faq.q: P vs NP — should I care practically?
faq.a: Yes as a triage skill: recognizing NP-hardness early saves weeks of hunting for an efficient exact algorithm. The practical move is approximation, heuristics, or parameterized algorithms.

faq.q: What's the MIT 6-3 / CMU / Stanford spine here?
faq.a: The distilled core of three curricula: MIT's computation structures + algorithms, CMU's systems-and-theory spine, Stanford's core cross-walk. Each module maps topics to their canonical free references.

faq.q: How deep does the distributed systems material go?
faq.a: To 'implement Raft on a whiteboard and explain linearizability' depth — enough to reason about real systems (databases, queues, consensus) rather than just use them.
It's proof-heavy by design — that's the formal-methods half. IL-02/IL-20 build the math; IL-08 applies it to CS. Take those first if proofs are new.

faq.q: Greedy vs DP — how do I tell which applies?
faq.a: Try greedy first (simpler); then hunt for a counterexample. If greedy fails but subproblems overlap with optimal substructure, it's DP. The drills train this discrimination.
